record.program_name: 2016 Measure A Affordable Housing Bond (Housing Bond)
record.administering_agency: County of Santa Clara Office of Supportive Housing (OSH), Housing and Community Development Division
record.typical_award_size: $950 million general obligation bond approved November 8, 2016. As of October 2026 the Board had committed $879.2 million; 65 multifamily rental developments in 12 cities received about $747 million ($714.3 million in Supportive Housing Development Program rounds 1 through 14 and off-cycle awards plus $11.9 million acquisition loans and $90.5 million County acquisitions). Individual commitments range from $1.0 million (The Veranda, Cupertino, 19 units) to $42.3 million (Mosaic Court, Milpitas, 134 units); Gateway Tower (220 units, San Jose) revised January 13, 2026 to $25,560,000, about $116,182 per unit.
record.per_unit_cap: No published cap. Awards have averaged roughly $100,000 to $200,000 per unit in recent rounds; $116,182 per unit at Gateway Tower (2026).
record.affordability_requirement: Board goals by category: PSH for persons with disabling conditions, rapid rehousing units, ELI (30% AMI) and VLI (50% AMI) units, plus 300 mixed-income units and homeownership. 4,800 rental unit goal exceeded (5,255 goal units approved, 109%). Long-term County regulatory agreement recorded on each project.
record.next_deadline: No new application round. As of October 2026 the remaining $67.8 million is reserved for three developments on County-owned land and one affordable homeownership development (Branham Station, VTA TOD). About $6.4 million of program-generated income is available to recommit to multifamily rental projects.
record.layering_notes: santaclaracounty.gov subdomains (osh, asr, bhsd, news, files) returned HTTP 403 to automated access on 2026-11-07; records were built from the Board of Supervisors IQM2 legislative files (sccgov.iqm2.com), the County Housing Element, Santa Clara County Housing Authority documents, HCD and BOE pages. The County's November 3, 2026 implementation report (first annual report, year 10 of a 10-year plan) states the bond is nearly fully deployed: 65 approved rental developments with 6,846 units (2,693 supportive), 38 in operation, 17 under construction, four fully financed and six in predevelopment; $30.5 million in program-generated income received, $23.5 million recommitted. Measure A averaged about $6 of outside funding per $1 of County bond money and has been the standard local soft source behind 4% and 9% tax credit deals in Santa Clara County; in 2025, 11 County-funded projects won tax credit awards. Awards are made through the over-the-counter Supportive Housing Development Fund NOFA (see separate record) and paired with SCCHA project-based vouchers (3,000 plus PBVs deployed). Do not confuse with the November 4, 2025 Measure A, a five-eighths cent County sales tax for safety-net services that is not a housing fund. The Board is studying a future housing fund (June 2, 2026 report) but no successor measure is on the November 2026 ballot; the statewide $10 billion housing bond (AB 736/SB 417) is the near-term pipeline source. County loans require state prevailing wage as public funds.
record.audit_note: Tier 4 Nov 9, 2026: core figures match the November 2026 implementation report ($950M bond, $879.2M committed, about $747M to 65 rental developments, $714.3M multifamily commitments, $67.8M remaining for three County-owned sites and Branham Station, $6,375,672 program income available for multifamily). Project-level figures (Veranda, Mosaic Court, Gateway Tower, acquisition loans) are not in this file but are not contradicted. prevailing_wage_trigger is uncited (no prevailing_wage_basis); the value rests on the general Labor Code 1720(b) public funds definition, not a program rule.

record.program_name: Supportive Housing Development Fund NOFA (SHDF NOFA)
record.administering_agency: County of Santa Clara Office of Supportive Housing (OSH)
record.typical_award_size: Single over-the-counter solicitation that consolidates all County-controlled housing production funds since 2017 (current NOFA issued August 16, 2021). Sources: 2016 Measure A bond, No Place Like Home (County is an alternative county with a direct allocation of $106,085,749 over four rounds; $102.9 million committed), the $40 million I/DD Housing Fund, Stanford Affordable Housing Fund, HOME (about $1 million a year; $3,269,475 programmed for FY 2026-27), CDBG (site acquisition), PLHA, Local Housing Trust Fund match and Homekey+ (over $40 million awarded in 2025-26 for Algarve Apartments with Abode). Measure A acquisition and predevelopment loans were capped at $8 million.
record.per_unit_cap: Not published. Underwriting guidelines are reviewed annually against state and federal capital sources.
record.affordability_requirement: Priority on extremely low-income and special needs households: homeless and chronically homeless, seniors, transition-age youth, agricultural workers, persons with disabilities. Since 2015 the County has funded 7,183 units, 2,997 set aside for homeless households.
record.next_deadline: Over the counter, no fixed deadline. With Measure A nearly committed, new awards depend on program income, NPLH interest, HOME, PLHA and state awards; the County Housing Element lists the SHDF NOFA as ongoing through 2031.
record.layering_notes: santaclaracounty.gov subdomains (osh, asr, bhsd, news, files) returned HTTP 403 to automated access on 2026-11-07; records were built from the Board of Supervisors IQM2 legislative files (sccgov.iqm2.com), the County Housing Element, Santa Clara County Housing Authority documents, HCD and BOE pages. The NOFA is the single door for County capital in Santa Clara County; applications are underwritten by OSH and taken to the Board in numbered rounds (Round 14 on May 20, 2025) or as off-cycle items. SCCHA project-based vouchers are awarded alongside County capital, and MTW Activity 2016-2 lets SCCHA attach PBVs without a separate competition to projects selected through the County NOFA within the last 15 years. OSH also manages a County Managed Housing Production Pipeline with the 15 cities and SCCHA, supports applications to CTCAC, CDLAC and HCD, and funded 11 tax credit awards in 2025. The County loan portfolio exceeds $1 billion across more than 12,000 units. Source is the County 2023-2031 Housing Element Program 1.01, supplemented by the March 17, 2026 HLUET annual report (sccgov.iqm2.com/Citizens/Detail_LegiFile.aspx?ID=127742) and the October 20, 2026 funding commitments item (ID=130362).
eligible_project_detail: housing for persons with intellectual and developmental disabilities

record.next_deadline: No open round as of November 8, 2026. No application process; AHF uses are approved by the Board case by case as loan modifications or preservation proposals are presented.

record.program_name: Stanford Affordable Housing Fund (SAHF)
record.administering_agency: County of Santa Clara Office of Supportive Housing (OSH); allocations approved by the Board of Supervisors
record.typical_award_size: Special revenue fund of in-lieu fees paid by Stanford University under the 2000 General Use Permit ($20 to $80 per square foot of academic floor area). $55.9 million collected since 2000; $61.3 million with interest; $1.7 million uncommitted as of June 30, 2026. Fees partially funded 423 new units in seven projects and preserved 237 units in two projects (660 units), with 250 more planned; awards have also gone to San Mateo County projects ($1.5 million, 965 Weeks Street, East Palo Alto).
record.per_unit_cap: None published. GUP fees have covered about 8.8 percent of total development cost in assisted projects.
record.affordability_requirement: Lower-income affordable housing within a six-mile radius of the Stanford campus; County regulatory agreement.
record.next_deadline: None. Apply through the SHDF NOFA; only $1.7 million remains uncommitted and the 2023 Stanford Community Plan removed the in-lieu fee pathway, so no new revenue is expected unless the Board restores it in the 2026 GUP.
record.layering_notes: santaclaracounty.gov subdomains (osh, asr, bhsd, news, files) returned HTTP 403 to automated access on 2026-11-07; records were built from the Board of Supervisors IQM2 legislative files (sccgov.iqm2.com), the County Housing Element, Santa Clara County Housing Authority documents, HCD and BOE pages. Stanford has asked that an in-lieu option be restored in the pending 2026 GUP; the Board has not decided. Treat as exhausted for underwriting until that decision.

record.program_name: Project-Based Vouchers, Santa Clara County Housing Authority (Moving to Work agency)
record.administering_agency: Santa Clara County Housing Authority (SCCHA)
record.typical_award_size: SCCHA assists over 22,000 households and has deployed more than 3,000 project-based vouchers to Measure A developments, leveraging about $415 million and anticipating over $3 billion in HAP payments over 20-year contracts. FY 2027 MTW Annual Plan lists 495 vouchers to be newly project-based at 10 properties: 1510 N. First St (57, RAD rehab), 245 Weddell (60), Clara Gardens (30), East Santa Clara Senior (20), Gateway Tower (65), Mountain View Lot 12 (35), Rincon de los Esteros (120, SCCHA acquisition), Trillium (36), Terra Bella (23) and VTA Berryessa (49). Typical award is 20 to 65 PBVs per development, 25 to 50 percent of units.
record.per_unit_cap: MTW modified PBV contract rents; payment standards up to SCCHA exception levels. PBV program cap raised to 40 percent of baseline vouchers under MTW Activity 2020-1.
record.affordability_requirement: PBV units serve households referred through coordinated entry (chronically homeless), families, seniors, veterans (HUD-VASH) and persons with disabilities; 20-year HAP contracts with County and SCCHA covenants.
record.next_deadline: No open PBV RFP. PBVs are awarded with County SHDF NOFA capital; MTW Activity 2016-2 allows non-competitive PBV selection for projects chosen through a federal, state or local government solicitation within the last 15 years. SCCHA procurement moved to PlanetBids (portal 66280) in 2026.
record.layering_notes: santaclaracounty.gov subdomains (osh, asr, bhsd, news, files) returned HTTP 403 to automated access on 2026-11-07; records were built from the Board of Supervisors IQM2 legislative files (sccgov.iqm2.com), the County Housing Element, Santa Clara County Housing Authority documents, HCD and BOE pages. PBVs are the operating backbone of Santa Clara County deals: Measure A capital plus SCCHA PBVs plus 4% credits is the standard stack, and the PBV HAP supports permanent debt sized to contract rents. Owners must certify that prevailing wages were paid for any work before HAP execution and that NEPA (24 CFR 50/58) was cleared before site work; HUD Davis-Bacon applies to PBV new construction or rehabilitation of nine or more contract units. SCCHA owns and acquires properties directly (Activity 2010-4, non-competitive PBVs for SCCHA-owned projects) and partners with the County on County-owned sites. The HCV interest list opened December 2020; SCCHA jurisdiction covers the whole county including San Jose (the former Housing Authority of the City of San Jose is administered by SCCHA).
record.audit_note: Tier 4 spot check Nov 9, 2026: FY2027 MTW Annual Plan confirms 22,000 households, 3,000+ PBVs, $415M leveraged, $3B HAP, the 10-property 495 PBV table, Activity 2016-2 (non-competitive selection within 15 years) and Activity 2020-1 (40% PBV cap). The plan table marks 1510 N. First as not RAD (a separate RAD conversion is discussed). Prevailing wage true is uncited.

record.program_name: Continuum of Care CA-500 (San Jose/Santa Clara City and County) and HHAP funding
record.administering_agency: County of Santa Clara Office of Supportive Housing (OSH) as CoC lead and collaborative applicant; City of San Jose and the CoC are co-applicants for HHAP
record.typical_award_size: HHAP Round 6 allocations (HCD, based on the 2024 PIT count): Santa Clara County $11,860,491.01; San Jose/Santa Clara City and County CoC $12,667,208.31; City of San Jose $25,329,964.46. The County's delegated HHAP-6 authority is $24,528,000 (County plus CoC shares); the state notified the region of its award March 17, 2026. The County is also administering about $10 million HHAP-2, $28 million HHAP-3, $25.8 million HHAP-4 and $27.9 million HHAP-5. HUD CoC program grants to the County total about $35.1 million for 23 renewals (2026-27) and the region receives roughly $48 million a year; the 2026 CoC competition application authority is up to $38.1 million for 24 grants.
record.per_unit_cap: Not applicable; operating and services funding.
record.affordability_requirement: Households experiencing homelessness referred through coordinated entry; Housing First required by the regional MOU; at least 10 percent of HHAP for youth.
record.next_deadline: HHAP-6 obligation and expenditure deadlines run through June 30, 2030 under the amended agreement. HUD vacated its 2026 CoC NOFO after federal litigation; the County delegated authority to apply for up to 24 CoC grants when the competition reopens.
record.layering_notes: santaclaracounty.gov subdomains (osh, asr, bhsd, news, files) returned HTTP 403 to automated access on 2026-11-07; records were built from the Board of Supervisors IQM2 legislative files (sccgov.iqm2.com), the County Housing Element, Santa Clara County Housing Authority documents, HCD and BOE pages. The County uses HHAP for the Homelessness Prevention System, interim housing operations and supportive services for permanent housing, not capital. For a PSH deal the practical asks are a CoC or County services contract and PBVs; the County has committed to fund supportive services at every Measure A development. HUD's proposed 30 percent cap on permanent housing in the 2026 CoC round puts about 1,600 PSH households at risk per OSH (October 2025 coverage). The 2026-2030 Community Plan to End Homelessness (endorsed September 15, 2026) sets a goal of housing 15,000 people. HHAP-6 allocation table opened at hcd.ca.gov (hhap-6-allocations.pdf).

record.program_name: Behavioral Health Services Act (BHSA) Integrated Plan FY 2026-27 through FY 2028-29, housing interventions
record.administering_agency: County of Santa Clara Behavioral Health Services Department (BHSD)
record.typical_award_size: Total BHSA expenditure budget about $160 million a year; Housing Interventions component at the statutory 30 percent, $48 million a year (no transfer or exemption requested). Uses: tenant-based rental assistance for up to 700 individuals a year (500 permanent, 200 interim), continuation of the Casa de Novo interim housing program, Transitional Rent and Housing Deposits as a Medi-Cal managed care plan contracted provider from January 1, 2026, and licensed residential care facility support through a separate $8,038,653 CCE Preservation grant ($4,578,568 capital, $3,460,085 operating).
record.per_unit_cap: Not applicable. The plan funds no project-based units (units funded per year reported as 0).
record.affordability_requirement: BHSA-eligible adults with serious mental illness or substance use disorder who are homeless or at risk; 50 percent of housing funds targeted to chronically homeless individuals, with a focus on encampments.
record.next_deadline: Draft Integrated Plan adopted by the Board June 2, 2026 and submitted to DHCS by June 30, 2026; plan period July 1, 2026 to June 30, 2029. Annual updates each spring.
record.layering_notes: santaclaracounty.gov subdomains (osh, asr, bhsd, news, files) returned HTTP 403 to automated access on 2026-11-07; records were built from the Board of Supervisors IQM2 legislative files (sccgov.iqm2.com), the County Housing Element, Santa Clara County Housing Authority documents, HCD and BOE pages. Santa Clara County elected not to use BHSA for capital development (the plan says MHSA housing funds go to interventions that provide more immediate access) and not to fund operating subsidies with BHSA, so unlike San Diego or Sacramento there is no BHSA capital or PSH operating line to underwrite here. BHSD contracts with two providers for on-site specialty mental health services at PSH developments and will refer BHSA clients to County and SCCHA project-based units through coordinated entry. The Casa de Novo site (Homekey) continues as interim housing. Plan PDF: sccgov.iqm2.com/Citizens/FileOpen.aspx?Type=4&ID=270066 (Attachment B). Audit 2026-11-08 funding_type: classed as grant because the Housing Interventions component funds tenant-based rental subsidies for housing (up to 700 individuals a year); there is no capital line and 0 project-based units, so it is not a development source.

record.program_name: Conduit multifamily and nonprofit housing bonds, County TEFRA approvals (CSCDA, CMFA)
record.administering_agency: County of Santa Clara Board of Supervisors; TEFRA hearings delegated to the Director of Finance
record.typical_award_size: The County does not issue its own multifamily housing bonds; it is a member of CSCDA (joined July 13, 1993) and approves conduit issues for projects in unincorporated territory or multi-site plans. 2026 example: CSCDA plan of finance up to $125,000,000 for Odd Fellows Home of California (Saratoga Retirement Community, $110 million, plus a Napa facility), approved February 24, 2026 after a February 4, 2026 teleconference TEFRA hearing. Affordable projects inside cities obtain TEFRA approval from the city council (for example CMFA issues for Sunnyvale Block 15, Sango Court in Milpitas, Santa Clara Apartments $33.5 million CDLAC allocation in 2026). SCCHA itself used CMFA for the Laurel Grove Lane acquisition.
record.per_unit_cap: Not applicable; sized by CDLAC allocation and the 50 percent test.
record.affordability_requirement: Federal 20 percent at 50 percent AMI or 40 percent at 60 percent AMI plus CDLAC requirements; County approval carries no additional covenant.
record.next_deadline: None. TEFRA hearings are held by Administration before the Board meeting at which the approval resolution is placed on the consent calendar; allow four to six weeks.
record.layering_notes: santaclaracounty.gov subdomains (osh, asr, bhsd, news, files) returned HTTP 403 to automated access on 2026-11-07; records were built from the Board of Supervisors IQM2 legislative files (sccgov.iqm2.com), the County Housing Element, Santa Clara County Housing Authority documents, HCD and BOE pages. Expect to go to CMFA, CSCDA or CalHFA for bonds and to the host city for TEFRA. The County's role is procedural and fee-free (the County incurs no cost or liability). SCCHA historically issued its own housing bonds (Blossom River 1998A still outstanding) but now acts as borrower through CMFA. Conduit bonds alone do not trigger state prevailing wage; County, state or federal subsidy in the same deal does.
record.audit_note: Tier 4 spot check Nov 9, 2026: IQM2 file 127492 (BOS-2026-25) confirms the CSCDA plan of finance up to $125,000,000 for Odd Fellows Home of California, adopted Feb 24, 2026 after a Feb 4, 2026 teleconference TEFRA hearing, County CSCDA membership since July 13, 1993, and the 2020 delegation to hold TEFRA hearings before the Board meeting. Prevailing wage false is uncited.

record.program_name: Gap Financing Program, rolling Request for Proposals with Notice of Funding Availability addenda (new construction and preservation)
record.administering_agency: City of San Jose Housing Department, Residential Development, Production and Preservation
record.typical_award_size: Construction-permanent and acquisition loans from the Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund, Inclusionary Fee Fund, Measure E Real Property Transfer Tax Fund and impact fee funds. The April 14, 2025 joint New Construction/Preservation RFP was backed by a $50 million commitment; the June 2025 Round 1 NOFA addendum has produced three awards so far. 2025 awards: $48.3 million for Berryessa TOD and Gateway Tower (415 units); Gateway Tower $38.44 million total ($174,727 per unit on 220 units, later revised to $25.56 million after CalHFA MIP and state credits); 1510 North 1st Street hotel conversion $5.7 million (58 units, October 2026); Capitol Station $8.4 million LMIHAF. Since January 2023 the City has provided $222.7 million to 16 developments producing 1,639 units.
record.per_unit_cap: No published cap. Recent per-unit City subsidy ranged from about $100,000 (1510 North 1st, with project-based vouchers) to $174,727 (Gateway Tower before state awards).
record.affordability_requirement: City affordability covenant of at least 55 years, senior to any deed of trust. Rolling RFP prioritizes construction-ready developments, extremely low and very low income units, permanent supportive housing with County vouchers, and preservation of at-risk units. Preservation NOFA target is $5 million average per year (Housing Element Program R-2).
record.next_deadline: Second NOFA addendum to the rolling RFP was planned for Q2 2026 and waitlisted applications refreshed; confirm the current addendum and submission window with the Housing Department (Banu San, Deputy Director, 408-975-4489). The RFP document is hosted on Biddingo and requires registration.
record.layering_notes: The primary local gap lender in the county alongside County Measure A (now fully committed, see county record). Staff align awards with County OSH funds and Santa Clara County Housing Authority project-based vouchers ($47.4 million County funds and 298 PBVs leveraged in 2025). Typical stack: 4 percent credits and bonds (City can be issuer under Policy 1-16 or CMFA/CSCDA), CalHFA MIP, AHSC, County SHDF, then City gap loan. The City's August 2026 alternative financing frameworks (see separate record) let staff combine gap financing with inclusionary projects and master-lease structures. Measure E dollars for new development were sharply reduced in the FY 2025-26 budget, so LMIHAF program income ($22.5 million deposited in FY 2024-25) and inclusionary in-lieu fees are the main recurring sources. sanjoseca.gov returns 403 to automated access; all documents were read from the Legistar attachment host.
record.cycle_notes: NOFA addenda to a rolling RFP, roughly annual

record.program_name: Measure E Real Property Transfer Tax (Municipal Code Chapter 4.59) and Council Policy 1-18 Section 22 spending allocations
record.administering_agency: City of San Jose Housing Department and City Manager's Budget Office; Real Property Transfer Tax Fund
record.typical_award_size: Transfer tax on sales above $2.3 million (threshold indexed from $2 million as of July 1, 2025): 0.75 percent from $2 million to $5 million, 1.0 percent from $5 million to $10 million, 1.5 percent above $10 million. About $225 million collected July 2020 through mid 2023. FY 2025-26 revenue estimate $55.0 million, FY 2026-27 $60.0 million. Original policy (April 2022) directed 40 percent to extremely low income housing, 30 percent low income, 5 percent moderate income, 10 percent homelessness prevention, 15 percent homeless support. The June 10, 2025 revision allows up to 90 percent of revenue after 5 percent administration for homeless sheltering and interim housing, with only the remainder for new or preserved affordable housing; the FY 2025-26 plan puts $0 of new revenue into affordable housing development. Prior-year Measure E reserves are still being drawn for development, for example $14 million for the Gateway Tower land acquisition (September 2025).
record.affordability_requirement: When used for development: new or preserved rental housing for extremely low (30 percent AMI) and low income households under City regulatory agreements; previously set by AMI category in Policy 1-18 Section 22.
record.next_deadline: No standalone Measure E NOFA. Future allocations for affordable housing depend on the FY 2026-27 budget (June 2026) and later budgets; shifts between 15 and 90 percent for shelter can be made without the 60-day notice and two-thirds vote. Verify remaining Measure E reserve balances with the Housing Department.
record.layering_notes: Measure E was the City's largest discretionary housing source from 2020 to 2024 and funded many Gap Financing Program awards. Expect limited new Measure E development money through at least FY 2026-27 because the General Fund shortfall shifted $39.2 million (rising to $42.8 million) of homelessness costs into this fund. Developers should underwrite LMIHAF and inclusionary fee funds first and treat Measure E as upside. A Measure E transfer tax refund pilot for qualifying nonprofit purchases (Section 4.59.230) ran July 2021 through June 30, 2024 with one application; it is now expired. Documents read via Legistar attachments because sanjoseca.gov is blocked. Audit 2026-11-08 funding_type: classed as loan because the development share reaches projects as Gap Financing Program loans (the June 2025 memo cites about $60 million of prior-year Measure E and other housing funds for a Gap Financing NOFA); the shelter share is City-operated spending, not a developer source.

CLF (Ordinance 30475, September 22, 2020): FY 2025-26 rates are $17.86 per square foot for office at or above 100,000 square feet downtown and nearby (lower tiers for smaller office), hotel $5.95, industrial over 100,000 square feet $3.57, warehouse $5.95, residential care $7.15, with reduced rates outside downtown. The CLF was adopted at well below the Keyser Marston nexus maximum and office construction has been weak, so expect only a few million dollars a year. The AHIF was replaced by extending the Inclusionary Housing Ordinance to rental projects of 10 or more units. record.program_name: Alternative financing frameworks for affordable housing (Gap Financing plus IHO, PAB plus master-lease, production incentives plus master-lease)
record.administering_agency: City of San Jose Housing Department
record.typical_award_size: Council resolution of September 1, 2026 authorizing the Housing Director to implement four mixed-financing models: (1) Gap Financing Program loans in exchange for deeper inclusionary set-asides (example: 10 percent of units at 50 percent AMI instead of 5 percent at 60 and 5 percent at 80); (2) private activity bonds combined with master-lease financing; (3) production incentive programs (MHIP) combined with master-lease financing; (4) master-lease financing combined with the Inclusionary Housing Ordinance. Target rents 40 to 110 percent AMI. No new dollars; uses existing Gap Financing, bond and incentive tools.
record.affordability_requirement: Varies by model; 40 percent AMI up to 110 percent AMI with recorded restrictions; Model 1 limited to tower and wrap projects already paying prevailing wage.
record.next_deadline: Housing Director may implement without further Council action subject to funding approvals; individual loan or master-lease commitments still return to Council. No deadline.
record.layering_notes: Relevant to developers of mixed-income towers (prevailing wage already assumed) and to nonprofit or public master lessees. Models borrow from the Bay Area Housing Finance Authority and CalHFA middle-income work; they will compete with the Multifamily Housing Incentive Program pipeline for the same market-rate projects. Prohousing: San Jose applied for HCD Prohousing Designation in June 2023 (memo read); current designation status was not confirmed this pass, verify on HCD's designated jurisdictions list. sanjoseca.gov blocked; memo read from Legistar. Audit 2026-11-08 funding_type: classed as loan because Model 1 is a Gap Financing loan and the master-lease models use City funding expected to be repaid on exit; no new grant dollars.

record.program_name: Affordable housing over-the-counter Notice of Funding Availability (Housing Impact Fund, BMR In-Lieu Fees Fund, Local Housing Trust Fund grant)
record.administering_agency: City of Mountain View Housing Department and Council NOFA Review Committee
record.typical_award_size: Over-the-counter (first come, first served) NOFA since 2014 funded by the Housing Impact Fee on office, high-tech, hotel and retail development, BMR in-lieu fees, and state Local Housing Trust Fund matching grants. Since 2014 the City has invested $119 million in affordable housing. Examples: Lot 12 (120 units, Alta Housing and Related California) $23.45 million total City commitment including $6.3 million BMR in-lieu, $5.95 million Housing Impact Fees, $3.2 million LHTF, $1.86 million HOME and $0.78 million HOME-ARP; 96 West El Camino Real (79 units, Danco) Housing Impact Fund $6.73 million plus $1.27 million PLHA; 1012 Linda Vista $10 million reservation (2023) returned to the funds in October 2025 pending a new NOFA application for a 53-unit version. City funding is targeted to 20 percent of total development cost (a $1 City to $4 other leverage ratio). Housing Element Program 4.3 commits about $40 million over the cycle; the pipeline gap was estimated at $50 million in 2024.
record.per_unit_cap: No fixed cap; City target is 20 percent of total development cost. Recent commitments equal roughly $85,000 to $195,000 per unit.
record.affordability_requirement: Multi-Family Rental Underwriting Guidelines (2022); deed restrictions for extremely low, very low and low income households; priority to projects that leverage County Measure A, PBVs and state funds and that serve unhoused and special needs households.
record.next_deadline: Applications accepted at any time; City-owned sites (Lot 12, 87 East Evelyn) are awarded by RFQ/RFP instead. An online application portal was targeted for late 2025. The Housing Impact Fee update is underway through a County collaborative nexus study; watch for a 2026 or 2027 fee action.
record.layering_notes: Mountain View has the strongest city housing fund in the county outside San Jose thanks to office linkage fees. Stack order used by staff: County Measure A or SHDF, SCCHA PBVs, 4 percent credits and CMFA bonds, state LHTF, PLHA and PIP pass-throughs, then City Housing Impact Fund and BMR funds last. The 2019 City-County MOU allocates Measure A to the City pipeline. The City also committed $4 million toward a $20 million acquisition and preservation pool for CSFRA rent-stabilized units (March 2024), contingent on $16 million in outside partners. mountainview.gov blocked; memos read from Legistar.

record.program_name: Non-Residential Housing Mitigation Fee (Housing Impact Fee), Municipal Code Chapter 19.75
record.administering_agency: City of Sunnyvale Community Development Department, Housing Division
record.typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Fee on new office, R&D, industrial, retail and lodging square footage in any zone since 2015; over $47 million collected 2015 to 2022. Fee revenue will slow with the office downturn, so the 2026 NOFA ($18 million) is smaller than 2024. Compare with San Jose's CLF ($6.1 million cumulative) and Mountain View's Housing Impact Fee. sunnyvale.ca.gov blocked; staff report read from Legistar.
